proof.criterion: Review finding 3 (blocking, Security[authz]): one unauthenticated source address could hold the whole fleet's reread route at zero, because the shared bucket refilled more slowly than one address was allowed to sustain, and an emptied shared bucket means no narrowing retag reaches any pod.
proof.surface: The three constants and their derivation, sized from the providers' own quotas as the architect ruled rather than from parity with one pod.
proof.command: cd packages/envoy && go test -tags multiprocess -count=1 -timeout 20m -v -run 'TestTwoBrokers/7' ./cmd/broker (the fleet budget row), with the ordering checked by arithmetic against the live constants
proof.observed: DefaultRereadLimit is {Every: 8s, Burst: 30}, derived as half the rate of the tighter shared bucket (2 × GCPRereadOverallLimit.Every) rather than chosen: 0.125 rereads a second per address against a shared 0.25/s on Secret Manager and 1/s on the default store, so two addresses are needed to starve the first and eight the second — the ordering this route had before the fan-out existed (0.5/s per address against 1/s and 4/s). At four pods the shared rates divide by sixteen and this one follows to 32 s; the comment says all three are re-derived together. The budgets are now cited: Secret Manager serves 600 read requests a minute per project (cloud.google.com/secret-manager/quotas) and this route takes a fifth of it, the rest being every pod's five-minute reload, its miss-path rereads and its releases, which the fan-out also multiplies; AWS serves DescribeSecret at 40,000 a second per Region (docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/asm.html), so the default bucket's budget is the broker's own policy writer lock and not a provider's cap at all. Raising the shared bucket instead was refused: the issue's acceptance line and row 7 both hold the fleet to one pod's old budget, so the ordering had to be restored from the per-address side. Row 7 still passes, since it constrains the shared rate, which did not move.
proof.negativeControl: The ordering is the assertion: before this change one address's 0.5 rereads a second outpaced the GCP shared bucket's 0.25 a second refill, which is the arithmetic the reviewer measured and the reason the finding was raised; after it, 0.125 is strictly below both shared refills with a factor of two to spare on the tighter one. What the change does not fix is stated in the comment rather than implied: one address can still spend the shared burst at once, as it always could, because a burst is a depth and the per-address burst has always been the larger.

proof.criterion: Review finding 2 (blocking): a SIGTERM during boot could no longer stop the pod at all — both boot calls ran on a context no signal cancels, and the second-signal escape was registered inside the drain, so a pod held a bound socket with no server behind it until SIGKILL at a grace period this change asks to be at least 65 s.
proof.surface: The compiled broker binary, started by hand against a real Postgres with its boot deliberately parked, signalled with kill -TERM and read from its own log and its exit status.
proof.command: go build -o /tmp/broker-manual/broker ./cmd/broker, then three scripted runs: one SIGTERM on a healthy boot; two SIGTERMs during the drain; and one and two SIGTERMs while the boot was parked in a secret-store read that honours no context (a FIFO with no writer as BROKER_FAKE_SECRETS_FILE)
proof.observed: Two SIGTERMs while the boot was parked: the process exited 1 the instant the second arrived, logging 'broker: a second signal arrived while the broker was still starting up, so it is stopping without a drain: it has served nothing'; on the code the review read, both signals were swallowed and the process had to be SIGKILLed. One SIGTERM in the same place: the process finished that stage and returned cleanly, status 0, logging 'broker: signalled while starting up, before it had bound anything stage="the first policy load"', with nothing listening on its port — it bound no socket and ran neither the drain nor the 60-second shutdown budget. Two SIGTERMs during a drain: the 20-second drain ended 1.0 s in on the second signal and the process still exited 0, so hoisting the channel out of the drain did not cost the drain its early exit. A healthy boot with one SIGTERM still drains its full budget and exits 0. The pieces: the signal channel is registered immediately after signal.NotifyContext and held for the process's life; a watchdog goroutine takes the first delivery and then either stands aside (serveStarted closed, so the drain reads the second signal) or logs and exits; oauthStore.Secret, the one boot call after the bind, is bounded by oauthSecretTimeout (10 s); and policy.NewCurrent, which cannot take a timeout because it hands the same context to its five-minute reload, is followed by an ctx.Err() test that returns.
proof.negativeControl: The same scripts against the previous head: both signals swallowed during the parked boot, the process still running when the script gave up. The healthy-boot and during-drain runs are the other control — the fix must not have turned an ordinary stop into an exit 1, and both still exit 0.

trickyParts: The three limits are now a derivation, not three numbers: the shared rate is the fleet's store budget divided by the replica count SQUARED (one accepted reread costs a store read on every pod), the shared burst by the replica count ALONE (a burst is a depth, and what it admits is one person's write burst, which the replica count does not change; what grows is each pod's own transient, its own burst plus every peer's), and the per-address rate is twice the tighter shared bucket's Every, so at least two addresses are needed to starve the fleet. Changing the replica count re-derives all three, and whether the ordering still holds is what says it was done.

A second signal has two readers, and which one takes it is decided by serveStarted, closed just before go srv.Serve. Before it the watchdog exits the process; after it the drain's select ends the drain. If both were ready at the same instant Go's select would pick either, but both outcomes stop the process and the one the race could pick is the one the second signal asked for.

policy.NewCurrent cannot be given a timeout: it hands the same context to its five-minute reload goroutine, so a bound there would kill the reload. That is why the first policy load is followed by a ctx.Err() test rather than wrapped, and why the second-signal watchdog is what covers a load that hangs.

cmd/agent-secrets/secret_e2e_test.go is the broker-wide burst's pin, named as such in limits.go. It is not a unit test of the constant: it drives the real client through three consecutive writes as a person does, and it is the product's promise that a write is served at once rather than at the next reload.
deviations: One change inside the tester's red row 7, at the reviewer's explicit request (thread PRRT_kwDORFy7ds6v-wkS): its counters are captured on the iteration the loop exits on rather than re-read afterwards. It removes a false-failure mode and weakens nothing; the comparison, the bounds and the budget figures are untouched, and the diff against the tester's commit shows only this and row 5's comment.

The architect asked whether the fleet bucket should grow rather than the per-address one shrink. It should not: the issue's own acceptance line and the tester's row 7 hold the fleet to what one pod was allowed, and the Secret Manager share this route takes is already only a fifth of the project's 600 a minute, the rest being the reloads, miss-path rereads and releases the fan-out also multiplies. The working is in the limits.go comments and in the thread reply.

The two paths this finding is about had to be parked elsewhere to be driven: a fake-secrets FIFO with no writer parks the boot in a read that honours no context, which is what exercises both the second-signal watchdog and the ctx.Err() return.
